extracted.intended_audience: students and members of the Royal Academy; aspiring painters and art students
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for the study and practice of painting in an academic (Royal Academy) setting: stages of learning, methods of copying and drawing from life, choice of models, work discipline, and how/when to depart from established rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit obedience to the rules of the great masters (for young students)
rubrics_metrics.description: “I would chiefly recommend that an implicit obedience to the rules of art, as established by the great masters, should be exacted from the young students. That those models, which have passed through the approbation of ages, should be considered by them as perfect and infallible guides as subjects for their imitation, not their criticism.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat established masterpieces as perfect guides during early training; learn by imitation rather than immediate criticism. Rules are a scaffold: only later, when the pupil is a master, may he 'take liberty to break through those rules.' Anti-pattern: starting with presuming on one's own sense and rejecting rules prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the three-stage progression of study
rubrics_metrics.description: Divides study into three periods: (1) rudiments — facility in drawing, management of colours, acquaintance with simple rules of composition; (2) collecting subjects and studying the masters to enlarge imagination; (3) emancipation — exercising independent judgment and discriminating perfections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect each stage: do not skip rudiments; in the second period consult many masters rather than one; in the third, trust your mature judgment to discriminate and innovate. The stages map to 'grammar' → 'vocabulary/stock of ideas' → 'original composition.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour, continual application and perseverance
rubrics_metrics.description: “Labour is the only price of solid fame ... there is no easy method of becoming a good painter.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect long, repetitive practice (an 'infinite number of acts') rather than quick talent shortcuts. Avoid dissipation and reliance on ephemeral praise. The recommended working method for major works: many sketches → finished drawing of whole → correct drawings of each part → paint → retouch from life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw exactly from the living model
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should 'draw exactly from the living models which they have before them' rather than altering form to fit vague ideas of beauty; their drawings should not 'resemble the model only in the attitude.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice precise, scrupulous copying from life to build exactness and a correct imagination. Benefit: 'a habit of drawing correctly what we see will not only give a habit of exactness and precision, but is continually advancing in his knowledge of the human figure.' Anti-pattern: drawing 'what they think the figure ought to be' rather than what appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer exact outline and correct drawing over flashy handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should 'contend who shall have the purest and most correct outline, instead of striving which shall produce the brightest tint' and should aim to give 'the most grace and dignity to the human figure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize solid draftsmanship, composition, and dignified treatment of figure and drapery rather than dazzling touch or brilliant but superficial effects. Anti-pattern: valuing 'a facility in composing, a lively, and ... masterly handling' above correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature dexterity and mechanical facility
rubrics_metrics.description: Premature 'masterly handling' and 'dazzling excellences' are 'frivolous pursuits' that debauch the mind and prevent later return to scrupulous labour; 'they take the shadow for the substance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct teaching to discourage praise of facile finish. Beware academies that reward despatch over correctness. Long-term harm: students reach 'utmost perfection' as boys and cannot advance to true excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy selectively: copy conceptions, not mechanical touches
rubrics_metrics.description: General copying is a 'delusive kind of industry'; instead 'copy only their conceptions. Instead of treading in their footsteps, endeavour only to keep the same road.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When copying a celebrated picture, select choice parts or the general machine/management of the composition. Use sketches of key ideas for later regulation of style. Anti-pattern: slavishly reproducing every brush-touch and finish of a master.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use side-by-side comparison with a master (make companion pieces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose painting a similar subject as a companion to a model, then placing them side-by-side to 'compare them carefully together' to see deficiencies more sensibly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This competitive comparison is a severe but effective method: it exposes faults, fixes principles by sensible objects, and strengthens self-teaching. Psychological note: requires humility and fortitude; it teaches better than passive copying or verbal precepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose models of established, age-tested reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Select works 'of established reputation rather than follow your own fancy' and prefer 'those great masters who have travelled the same road with success' rather than moderns who 'recommend themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the world's long-standing judgment guide selection of models. If you initially do not admire them, attempt imitation; the student's taste will be corrected. Anti-pattern: taking contemporary local painters who push themselves as the student's standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulate a broad stock of ideas: invention is recombination
rubrics_metrics.description: “Invention, strictly speaking, is little more than a new combination of those images which have been previously gathered and deposited in the memory. Nothing can come of nothing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend a great part of life collecting materials — subjects, incidents, appearances of nature, and the operations of the passions — so you can recombine them into invention. Travelling, looking widely at masters and life, and reading are necessary to avoid narrowness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying exclusively on mechanical practice or mere copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical practice and servile copying may give the appearance of progress but often result in incapacity to produce anything original; 'those powers of invention and composition ... lie torpid' under unthinking copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance technical exercises with thoughtful study of design, composition and nature. Do not mistake prolonged finished copies for true advancement. Use copying to learn specific devices (colour handling, contrasts), not as an end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study colouring by critical observation, but prefer nature
rubrics_metrics.description: An eye for colour is formed by observing well-coloured pictures and nature; however 'old pictures ... are often so changed by dirt and varnish' that unexperienced painters may be misled. 'You cannot do better than have recourse to nature herself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn colour through close examination of good pictures (to discover handling, glazing, contrasts), but cross-check with nature. Develop ability to 'see the brilliancy of tints through the cloud' of varnish and age. Anti-pattern: slavish imitation of an altered picture's surface appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directors/teachers must supervise advanced pupils closely
rubrics_metrics.description: The directors 'ought more particularly to watch over the genius of those students who, being more advanced, are arrived at that critical period of study' because they are tempted by brilliance and sloth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should identify the critical period when pupils prefer showy effects and intervene to redirect ambition toward exactness and serious study. Institutional responsibility: the academy must supply varied subjects so the method of exact drawing from life is effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work method for great compositions (sequence of preparation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When masters conceived a subject they 'first made a variety of sketches; then a finished drawing of the whole; after that a more correct drawing of every separate part, heads, hands, feet, and pieces of drapery; they then painted the picture, and after all re-touched it from the life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt this staged working process for important works: exploratory sketches → whole composition drawing → precise part drawings → paint → life retouching. This disciplined sequence guards against superficiality and supports painstaking excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not study too exclusively one master; consult many to avoid narrowness
rubrics_metrics.description: In the second period 'he is now to consider the art itself as his master... With a variety of models thus before him, he will avoid that narrowness and poverty of conception which attends a bigoted admiration of a single master.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose yourself to a variety of great masters and schools so you can combine perfections and avoid slavish imitation. Anti-pattern: bigoted admiration of a single master leading to limited conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-teaching through comparison yields deeper learning
rubrics_metrics.description: We learn best by being 'our own teachers' — attempting, comparing, and discovering faults ourselves; 'few have been taught to any purpose who have not been their own teachers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage practices that make students discover their own mistakes (comparisons, companion pictures, self-critique). Self-derived corrections are more effective and durable than externally imposed corrections alone.
